plot_arc.inciting_incident: Recording underneath high-tension power wires resulting in massive electrical hum and an apparent audio-video clock desync, kicking off an adventure into AI forensics and articles on verifiable competence.
plot_arc.rising_action: Prompting frontier models for audio restoration and watching them produce authoritative, hallucinated DSP pipelines and bogus drift ratios, followed by returning to the trail to re-attempt the physical scenario under the conductors.
plot_arc.climax: Constructing deterministic Python DSP notch filters and spectral gating to salvage the audio, verifying whether the filter was a brittle one-off or a reproducible general-purpose tool.
plot_arc.resolution: The cautionary realization that when AI models project fluent competence far beyond our ability to verify, sovereign testing and empirical ground truth are the only real safeguards against catastrophic failure.

narrative.core_inquiry: When AI models project effortless confidence across specialized technical domains, how does an experienced engineer determine where competence ends and plausible falsehood begins?
narrative.chicago_context: Echoes the early Chicago craftsmanship ethos: rejecting vendor marketing claims in favor of empirical, reproducible tests and shared practitioner honesty.
narrative.ai_era_parallel: The defining challenge of Staff+ engineering in 2026: maintaining cognitive control over system boundaries rather than passively accepting synthetic code generation. Grounded in the Watts synthesis: Alan Watts warned IBM engineers in 1969 not to mistake the net of discrete tokens for the living organism, while Peter Watts demonstrated in Blindsight that high-throughput symbol manipulation can simulate intelligence without comprehension.

teleprompter_script.act_1:
[SCENE: Cam on desk]
In October 2026 I walked out under 345,000-volt transmission lines in Northern Illinois
with a smartphone to record some thoughts on software craftsmanship.
When I got back to my desk and checked the footage, the audio was destroyed.
60 Hz electromagnetic hum. Corona arcing. And what looked like a three-and-a-half-minute
clock drift between audio and video.
[FREEFORM: Describe what it felt like sitting there staring at the waveform - the instinct to just trash it and reshoot]
The standard advice is: trash it, reshoot.
Instead, I opened a browser tab and started asking AI models what to do.
That's how this series started.
[PAUSE]
This is The Sound Above: Minus Zero. I'm Mike Hall.
The bottleneck in engineering is never generation. It's verification.
teleprompter_script.act_2:
[SCENE: Terminal - show the original prompt or a browser tab with the chat]
I started with thirteen words in a browser. Then brought it into Gemini Flash via the terminal.
The model immediately went to work.
Cascaded Butterworth filters. Exact duration ratios. Shell scripts. DSP pipelines.
It told me with total, unblinking confidence that the audio had drifted by twenty percent.
atempo=0.837. Here's the command. Run it.
[SHOW: The actual bad atempo command the model produced]
And it was completely wrong.
[FREEFORM: Talk about the sticker on the 2009 Dell Studio XPS from the Obtiva days: "Typing is not the bottleneck."
Talk about what that meant then vs what it means now - generating code is not the bottleneck, domain understanding is]
In Hollywood, they yell "Enhance!" and pixels appear from nowhere.
In software, that wishful thinking produces AI slop.
[PAUSE: let that sit]
The bottleneck is domain understanding. Same as it was in 2009.
teleprompter_script.act_3:
[SCENE: Show waveform or terminal output]
The container said: 21 minutes of video. 18 minutes of audio.
The model assumed linear drift and handed me atempo=0.837.
[SHOW: Audio waveform slurred - before fix]
When I tested it in headphones, the speech was slurred and completely out of sync.
[FREEFORM: Talk about what going back to ground truth feels like - the discipline of not trusting the answer just because it came out confidently]
So we went back to ground truth.
High-FPS frame extraction. Whisper subtitle alignment. Audio waveforms.
What had actually happened?
At 18 minutes I said "Thank you" and wrapped the talk.
The remaining three and a half minutes was me walking in silence with the camera still running.
The speech was at 1.0x the whole time.
[PAUSE]
When AI models project effortless competence, how do you find the boundary?
You verify with empirical tests. Not conversational trust.
teleprompter_script.act_4:
[SCENE: Show phone diagram or dual-mic diagram slide]
[SHOW: Diagram of iPhone dual-mic placement - top mic vs bottom mic]
Here's what was actually going on with the audio.
Modern smartphones use dual mics for noise suppression.
The mic at the top was acting as an unshielded inductive loop antenna.
Picking up 65 times more electromagnetic interference from the overhead towers
than the bottom mic.
[SHOW: Spectral waterfall - before and after isolating bottom mic]
Isolating the bottom mic gave us clean speech buried under the noise.
[FREEFORM: Talk about the decision to go back out under those same wires.
What you wanted to prove - was the dehum filter a one-time lucky fix or a real tool?]
And I didn't leave it there as a single lucky fix.
I walked back out under those same 345kV conductors.
Deliberately re-attempted the scenario. Same trail, same conductors.
I wanted to know: is this filter real, or was it one good day?
[SHOW: Second field recording footage if cued, or just the trail photo]
teleprompter_script.act_5:
[SCENE: Terminal - show the deterministic filter running]
[DEMO: Run the dehum filter against the second field recording - show timing output]
That field re-test gets to the heart of the cautionary tale.
When you prompt a frontier model outside your domain, it hands you math and code
with total, fluent confidence. You look like an audio engineering expert.
But you're throwing a ball high into the air.
If you throw it too high, far beyond what you can verify and catch,
it comes straight down on your head.
[SHOW: just3ws.localhost/dehum/dashboard.html - the A/B listening comparison]
[FREEFORM: Walk through what the dashboard shows - the raw audio, the hum-removed audio,
the spectral diff, the filter parameters that survived the second test]
When we ran the re-attempt footage through the same pipeline, the parameters held.
40 milliseconds. Stripped the hum. Preserved clean voice.
But the warning stands: AI models simulate mastery without comprehension.
Like the Chinese room in Peter Watts' Blindsight.
Our job isn't to marvel at synthetic fluency.
Our job is to walk back under the wires and test the boundary.

teleprompter_script.act_3:
[SCENE: Show WebSocket diagram or TypeScript server code]
[DEMO: Show the TypeScript engine structure - the intent handler, the state machine, the action ledger]
The real challenge was turning tabletop rules into a live multiplayer architecture.
Many game architectures make the mistake of trusting the client to resolve moves.
In Phalanx Duel, the client never dictates state.
It sends player intent over a WebSocket connection.
The server validates that intent against current deterministic state,
computes the next transition,
and records the exact action in an immutable ledger.
[FREEFORM: Talk about why client-authority is the wrong model for anything where integrity matters.
Connect it to the same problem in production systems: hidden state, unverifiable transitions,
no ground truth for what actually happened.]
What a table verifies with physical cards is what the server enforces on every turn.
The boundary is the same. The discipline is the same.
teleprompter_script.act_4:
[SCENE: Show role-safe projection diagram or the network protocol flow]
[SHOW: Slide or diagram - what Player 1 sees vs Player 2 sees vs Spectator sees]
Determinism is necessary but not sufficient.
An engine can be 100 percent deterministic while executing completely flawed logic.
To bridge that gap: replay fingerprints, action verification hashes, role-safe projections.
The authoritative server maintains complete match state, including facedown cards.
When broadcasting updates, it projects only what each role should see.
Player 1 gets their private hand. Player 2 gets theirs.
Spectators get a time-delayed broadcast.
[FREEFORM: Connect role-safe projections to information security in distributed production systems.
Talk about where you've seen the same problem in enterprise contexts: services that broadcast too much,
or clients that trust themselves to compute state they don't own.]
The protocol itself becomes an active guardian of the game's integrity.
